schemaVersion: Ehel Intensive English Course Plan v1.0
subject: English
audience: Adults and older teenagers of any first language, beginner to proficient, studying intensively
designModel: Grade 1 English — unit 0 sounds module, full-screen pattern carousel, one idea per screen, audio on every line

cefr.name: Common European Framework of Reference for Languages
cefr.role: Defines what a learner can DO at the end of each level, and therefore what each level's exit assessment tests. This is the framework the course reports against.
cefr.structure: Six CEFR levels collapse into five course levels: A1 and A2 combine into Level 1, and each level above is one CEFR level.

cambridge.name: Cambridge Primary English 0058 and Cambridge Lower Secondary English 0861
cambridge.role: Defines the language inventory, progression and text types, because the source material is built against it. Every outcome keeps the objective code of the source unit it came from.

frameworks.howTheyRelate: They are not the same axis and must not be treated as one. Cambridge grades measure a child progressing through school in English; CEFR levels measure what any user can do in a second language. A grade band supplies this course's language content; a CEFR level sets its target. The mapping below is a claim about what the compressed content delivers to an adult L2 learner, not a claim that grade N equals CEFR X.

sourceMaterial: src/prototypes/ehel-academy/english/grade-{1..8} — 81 units, 2212 vocabulary items, 486 grammar lessons. Analysis: inputs/ehel-english-intensive-source/grade-1-8-analysis.json
compressionPrinciple: Grades 1-8 teach 16 language patterns more than once, because children need spiral return. Adults do not. Each pattern is taught ONCE here, at the point it first becomes useful, and then recycled through later units' tasks rather than re-taught. That is where the 81-to-40 compression comes from — not from cutting language. A card that CONTRASTS patterns already taught is not a re-teach, but it must be flagged with "contrast": true so the duplication gate can allow it explicitly rather than by accident.
whatIsDropped: Child-world topics with no adult use (Fun and Games, All About Bugs, animal sounds, costumes) — their grammar is kept, their topic is replaced with an adult context that carries the same pattern.
Repeat teaching of a pattern already taught. The second and third pass become practice inside a later unit, not a grammar lesson.
Per-grade capstones (five of them across grades 1-4, five across 5-8) collapse into one capstone per level.

Whole-alphabet phonics. Adult learners arrive already literate in some script and mostly decoding Latin letters. Unit 0 teaches the sounds and syllable shapes that are hard in English, and lets the learner find out by testing themselves which of those are hard for them.

levels.label: Level 1 — Foundation

cefrBands.canDo: Understand and use basic words and set phrases for immediate needs, and interact slowly with a patient speaker.
Follow short, simple information and hold basic exchanges about familiar, everyday matters.

levels.exitDescriptor: Exits at a secure A2. Can handle everyday personal, practical and workplace situations: introduce themselves, describe people, places and routines, talk about the past and the future, follow and give instructions, ask for what they need, and write a short connected text.
levels.exitAssessment: A2 exit test across the four skills. Passing it is the entry condition for Level 2.

units.title: The Sounds That Are Hard
patterns: consonant clusters at the start and end of a word
long and short vowels: ship and sheep
blending: reading a word you have never seen
units.note: Not the whole alphabet. This unit teaches the six things learners most often find hard in English, and it opens with a self-check so the learner discovers which of the six are hard FOR THEM. Which ones those are depends on the learner's first language, and the course never assumes what that is.

units.title: Who I Am
patterns: I / you / he / she / it / we / they

units.title: Learning English
patterns: asking someone to repeat or slow down

units.title: Numbers, Money and Measuring
patterns: quantifiers: some, a lot of, a little

units.title: My Day, My Week
patterns: prepositions of time: at, on, in

units.title: Food, Markets and Cooking
patterns: units and containers: a packet of, a bottle of, a slice of
units.note: Countability itself is taught in Unit 4, through how much/how many and a little/a few. This unit APPLIES it to containers and measures rather than teaching it again.

units.title: The Body, Illness and the Clinic
patterns: saying what is wrong: I have got a …, my … hurts, I feel …
reading a medicine label: dose, frequency and warnings
units.note: Obligation (must, mustn't, have to) belongs to Unit 17, and the past simple to Unit 14, so this unit stays on symptom language, advice, and reading a label. Three patterns, not four.

units.title: Clothes, Colours and Buying Things
patterns: asking for a different one: size, colour or price
units.note: Asking a price is taught in Unit 4. This unit covers what you say AFTER the price — asking for a different size, colour or price.

units.title: Finding My Way
patterns: words for movement: along, past, across, through, towards
giving a route: turn, take, go straight on
asking the way politely: excuse me, could you tell me …?
units.note: Static place prepositions are taught in Unit 2 and imperatives in Units 3 and 6 — this unit APPLIES both to routes rather than teaching them again. It also owns polite requests, since it comes before Unit 18. Left and right are Unit 3 vocabulary and are recycled here, not re-listed.

units.title: Travel and Transport
patterns: present continuous: happening now and arranged for later
buying a ticket: times, platforms and returns
units.note: Owns the present continuous entirely — both the now use and the arranged-future use — so Unit 15 does not teach it again. Going to belongs to Unit 15.

units.title: Work and Jobs
patterns: have to and do not have to for obligation
adverbs of degree: very, quite, really
units.note: Third-person -s is taught in Unit 3 and the present simple in Unit 5; both are used here, not retaught. Wh- questions belong to Unit 16. This unit owns have to; must and mustn't belong to Unit 17.

units.title: Describing People and Things
units.note: Comparatives are taught in Unit 4, including more and the irregulars. This unit owns superlatives only.

units.title: Weather, Land and Water
patterns: will for prediction and for decisions
units.note: Owns will entirely, so Unit 15 contrasts it rather than teaching it. Present simple for facts is Unit 5 and is used here, not retaught.

units.title: Telling What Happened
patterns: past simple: the irregular verbs that matter
ago and last: the past time markers
units.note: The two past-simple cards are deliberate progression within one unit. Time markers are narrowed to the past-specific ones; at, on and in are Unit 5.

units.title: Plans and the Future
patterns: choosing between will, going to and the present continuous
arranging to meet: shall we, how about
units.note: Will is taught in Unit 13 and the present continuous in Unit 10. What is new here is choosing between the three, which is a genuine difficulty and not a re-teach. The contrast card names three forms taught in Units 10 and 13 and is flagged as a contrast rather than a re-teach: a card that only compares must be marked, because the duplication check cannot tell the difference and tuning it quiet would hide real collisions.
contrastPatterns: choosing between will, going to and the present continuous

units.title: Asking Well
units.note: Asking someone to repeat is Unit 3 and polite requests are Unit 9. This unit owns question FORM.

units.title: Instructions, Rules and Advice
patterns: allowed and not allowed: can, cannot, no + -ing
reading a public sign or safety notice
units.note: Should is Unit 7 and have to is Unit 11, so this unit owns must and mustn't only. Imperatives are Units 3 and 6 and sequencing is Unit 6; both are applied here, not retaught.

units.title: Getting Help and Getting Things Done
patterns: explaining a problem: it does not work, it is broken
filling in a form and making an appointment
units.note: Because and so are taught in Unit 13, so this unit adds so that for purpose only. Polite requests are Unit 9.

units.title: Level 1 Capstone — My English Life
patterns: finding your own errors: listen twice, sort into two lists
units.note: Replaces four separate per-grade capstones. Portfolio, spoken presentation, and the Level 1 exit assessment.

levels.label: Level 2 — Independence

cefrBands.canDo: Cope with routine situations, follow the main points of clear standard input, and produce simple connected text.
Sustain an argument, report what others said, and write formally for a real purpose — the bridge into B2.

levels.exitDescriptor: Exits at a secure B1 reaching towards B2. The learner becomes an independent user: can follow the main points of clear standard input, take part in extended discussion on familiar and unfamiliar topics, read and judge a source, report what other people said, write formally for a real purpose, and argue a position with support.
levels.exitAssessment: B1 exit test across the four skills. This is the level that matters commercially — it is where a learner becomes an independent user and qualifies for foundation and pathway steps.

units.title: Telling My Story
patterns: adjective + preposition: good at, interested in, worried about
used to for past habits and states that are now over
ordering a life story: by then, at that point, some years later

units.title: Saying It Precisely
patterns: ordering two or more adjectives: a small round wooden table
comparative adverbs: more carefully, better, faster
gradable and non-gradable adjectives: very cold, absolutely freezing
units.note: Comparatives are taught in grades 3, 5, 6 and 8 in the source. Once here.

units.title: Packing More Into a Sentence
patterns: non-defining relative clauses and the comma rule
relative clauses with where and whose

units.title: Joining Ideas
patterns: subordinating conjunctions beyond because and so
connective adverbs between sentences: however, therefore, moreover

units.title: Reporting What People Said
patterns: reported statements: tense and pronoun shift

units.title: The Passive Voice
units.note: The source teaches passive across grades 4, 6, 7 and 8. Once here, then used in the report-writing unit.

units.title: Narrating the Past
patterns: past continuous, with while, when and until
participle clauses: having finished, walking home

units.title: Verb Patterns
patterns: gerund and infinitive after a verb

units.title: Certainty and Possibility
patterns: modals of deduction: must be, might be, can't be
past modals: should have, could have, must have

units.title: Work, Careers and Applying
patterns: the language of a CV and a covering letter
answering an interview question with evidence

units.title: Money, Enterprise and Being a Customer
patterns: partitive expressions: a piece of, a bar of, a great deal of
the language of price, value and contract
making a complaint and asking for a remedy

units.title: Media, Technology and Judging a Source
patterns: vague attribution: sources say, it is understood, critics argue
discourse markers: actually, in fact, mind you

units.title: Environment and Resources
patterns: hedging a claim: tends to, is likely to, appears to
cause and effect chains: leads to, results in, is caused by
citing a source: according to, research suggests

units.title: Writing Formally
patterns: the formal letter, the email and the report
clauses ending with a preposition, and when to avoid them

units.title: Making an Argument
patterns: persuasive devices and their honest use

units.title: Level 2 Capstone — My English Voice
units.note: Replaces four per-grade capstones. Extended written piece, a presentation with questions, and the Level 2 exit assessment.

levels.label: Level 3 — Upper-Intermediate
levels.exitDescriptor: Can follow concrete and abstract discussion, interact with reasonable fluency, and write clear, detailed text on a range of topics. The common benchmark for many undergraduate courses and mixed-language workplaces.
levels.blockedBy: Grades 9-12 do not exist in this repository — English, Mathematics and Science all stop at grade 8. Level 3 cannot be planned in detail until that material is authored.

levels.label: Level 4 — Advanced
levels.exitDescriptor: Can use English flexibly for complex, demanding purposes and grasp implicit meaning in long, involved texts. Expected by many postgraduate courses and by roles built on persuasion or writing.
levels.blockedBy: C1 sits above the school curriculum this course compresses. Grades 9-12 will not reach it on their own — Level 4 needs its own source material (academic writing, extended argument, register control), which does not exist here and was not part of the grade 1-12 plan.

levels.label: Level 5 — Proficient
levels.exitDescriptor: Can understand almost everything read or heard and express fine shades of meaning precisely, at near-native command.
levels.blockedBy: Needs its own source material, as Level 4 does.
levels.note: Worth a commercial decision before it is built. C2 is rarely set as a minimum requirement by anyone — it marks the top of the scale rather than an entry point — so a five-level course may sell on completeness while almost nobody enrols in Level 5. Levels 2 and 3 (B1 and B2) are where the demand sits.

teachingLanguage: English. The course is monolingual: it explains English in English, at a level the learner can already read, so it works for a class with no shared first language.
selfTeaching: The course must be completable with no teacher present. Every exercise carries a learner-facing answer key, every task that would need a partner has a solo alternative, every practice is preceded by a worked example, and the learner diagnoses their own errors rather than waiting to be corrected. A teacher, where one exists, is an accelerator and never a dependency.
